clue.text: Accompanied by star, left behind with knowledge of Glasgow sports venue (10,4)

blocks.note: Scots — a Glaswegian's 'kenning' is knowledge, as in 'beyond my kennin'
as in singing to a piano — 'to' an accompaniment
an exploding star
L = left; 'behind' puts the whole TO-NOVA-L run after KENNING

explanation.walkthrough: Don't hunt for a Glasgow ground: the Oval is in London, and 'Glasgow' is only there to flag KENNING as Scots for knowledge. 'Behind' tells you the star-and-left assembly follows it.

clue.text: Charles and his mum in dust-up about constant sleazy activity (4,8)

blocks.note: King Charles — K…ING wraps round everything else
Elizabeth Regina, the late Queen's royal cypher
split round the constant
c — the speed of light, physics' favourite constant

explanation.walkthrough: Two containers at once: KING (Charles) wraps everything, and inside it the BRAWL wraps the C. ER = Elizabeth Regina is a convention worth learning — setters lean on royal cyphers constantly.

clue.text: Water nymph transformed by Diana (5)

blocks.note: the goddess supplies her own five letters

explanation.walkthrough: Diana's own letters rearrange into one of the nymphs who attended the goddess of the hunt — surface and wordplay are the same five letters.

clue.text: Mostly where soldiers are trained to place their trust (2,7)

definitions.text: where soldiers are trained to place their trust

blocks.note: the everyday adverbial sense: broadly speaking, without accounting for exceptions

blocks.clueFragment: where soldiers are trained to place their trust
blocks.note: whimsically, troops put their faith in (their) general

explanation.walkthrough: One word of definition, then the joke: soldiers are drilled to place their trust in their general.

clue.text: Harsh and unscrupulous activity, seizing racy tapes (7)

definitions.note: The answer is a noun — the Nazi secret police, and by extension any brutal enforcement outfit — defined here by its notorious qualities rather than by another noun.

blocks.note: on the go = active; G…O seizes the rest
the letters of TAPES, made 'racy' — shuffled

explanation.walkthrough: GO as in 'on the go'. The definition is really the Gestapo's reputation — and the surface, an outfit seizing tapes, is uncomfortably close to the literal truth.

clue.text: Awfully sick after leaving new soup kitchen, getting better (2,3,2)

blocks.note: the letters S, I, C, K — scattered ('awfully') through SOUP KITCHEN — depart
what is left of SOUP KITCHEN once SICK has gone

explanation.walkthrough: A deletion inside an anagram: 'awfully' licenses taking SICK's letters from wherever they sit in SOUP KITCHEN, and 'new' stirs what remains.

clue.text: Start rolling the cameras here (5)

blocks.note: the straight dictionary sense: a noun for the beginning of something
split into two words, this names the location on a film shoot where the cameras roll

explanation.walkthrough: A start, or where filming starts: on set. The second reading is the whimsical one, which is why it carries the cameras.

clue.text: Notices surrounding hip-hop doctor’s name on envelope (9)

blocks.note: the first of the two 'notices' — a small ad
Dr Dre's — sandwiched by the notices
…and the second: to see something is to notice it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Notices' is plural for a reason: the one word supplies two separate pieces, one at each end of the answer. Spotting that a single word does double duty is the step most solvers miss.

clue.text: Regretful of £1000 deposited after bankruptcy (5)

definitions.note: 'Ruing' is a participle and 'regretful of' an adjective phrase, but they swap cleanly — 'ruing the loss' means 'regretful of the loss' — so the definition is fair.

blocks.note: financial ruin
a grand — standard crossword currency

explanation.walkthrough: G for grand — £1000 — is a staple abbreviation; 'deposited after' banks it at the end of the ruin.

clue.text: Discarded top class team (3-5)

blocks.note: school streaming: the top class is Set A
a side, as in a football side

explanation.walkthrough: School streaming does the work — in many schools the top class is called Set A, and a side is a team in sport.

clue.text: Sorcerer welcomes assistance getting diplomat initial crossing? (6,6)

blocks.note: M…AGE, wrapped round the rest
help
an envoy

explanation.walkthrough: The sorcerer swallows both the help and the diplomat. 'Initial crossing' is the definition — a ship's first trip across the water.

clue.text: Solo turn by crossword guru touring centre of 1ac? (7)

blocks.note: Jonathan Crowther — Azed of the Observer, the setters' setter
the middle letter of ONE, which Azed 'tours' (wraps round): AZ-N-ED
the 'ac' tags along as letters; then the whole AZNED-AC does a turn

explanation.walkthrough: Azed took his pseudonym from Deza, a Spanish Grand Inquisitor, spelt backwards — so sending him round a turn is a fitting tribute. The question mark owns up to the liberties taken with '1ac'.

clue.text: Maximum and minimum values taken out of context, remarkably (7)

blocks.note: spelled out across the two words: contEXT REMArkably

explanation.walkthrough: 'Taken out of context' sounds like a complaint about quotation, but it is a literal instruction — the answer sits inside those letters.

clue.text: Change location of union meeting in telephone call? (5)

blocks.note: the union is a wedding, and the altar is where it happens

explanation.walkthrough: Weddings are the 'union' here, and 'in telephone call' tells you to listen rather than read: altar and alter sound the same.

clue.text: Actor suggesting a spot of 1dn? (3,6)

blocks.note: 'tom' is old slang for a prostitute — the one being crawled towards
and the same cross-reference again for the verb: to cruise is to drive slowly around looking for custom

explanation.walkthrough: The actor's name reads as a little kerb crawling: a tom on the cruise. The cross-reference to 1 down is the whole engine of the clue.

clue.text: Under a great burden, Ms Viner perhaps, with work (9)

blocks.note: op. — an opus; 'with' bolts it on at the front
Katharine Viner edits the Guardian: a press ed.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' concedes Ms Viner is only one example of a press ed. — any newspaper editor would do.

clue.text: Sort of alpine act a daring climb? (2,7)

blocks.note: nine letters to shuffle

explanation.walkthrough: El Capitan in Yosemite is the daring climb — famously scaled without ropes in Free Solo. 'Sort of' quietly does the shuffling.

clue.text: An essential for burner of midnight oil hit spot (9)

definitions.text: An essential for burner of midnight oil

blocks.note: to lam = to hit, as in 'lam into'
a spot — the tight kind

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are rougher than they look: to LAM is to hit, and the spot here is a PLIGHT. Burn the midnight oil and this is what you read by.

clue.text: It’s a bit gluey getting up on a cycle (7)

blocks.note: elating = uplifting, getting your spirits up

explanation.walkthrough: A rare device: 'on a cycle' means the letters rotate — push the G of ELATING from the back round to the front. Gelatin genuinely is the gluey bit: glue is made from it.

clue.text: Old drunkard beats wino up (7)

blocks.note: a wino is a SOT, sent climbing
beats = TOPS, also sent climbing

explanation.walkthrough: This is a down entry, so 'up' sends TOPS and SOT bottom-to-top together. 'Old' flags that tosspot is an archaic word for a drunkard.

clue.text: Guiltless about Jack Sprat’s diet, it’s implied (5)

blocks.note: c = circa, about
he could eat no fat — so what he did eat, by implication, was the lean

explanation.walkthrough: The nursery rhyme is the key: Jack Sprat could eat no fat, so his diet — never stated outright — was the lean.

clue.text: Arctic resident worked in retirement with supercomputer (7)

blocks.note: worked = RAN, sent backwards 'in retirement'
w = with
HAL 9000, the computer in 2001: A Space Odyssey

explanation.walkthrough: The tusked whale of the Arctic. HAL is cinema's most famous computer, and 'in retirement' — withdrawing — is a direction-neutral way to reverse RAN.

clue.text: Spurs are improving, reportedly (still in need of work) (5)

blocks.note: to heal is to mend, to get better
a parenthetical dig — even improving, Tottenham remain a work in progress — keeping you on the football reading of Spurs

explanation.walkthrough: A heel is the spur a fighting cock wears — the sense behind 'well-heeled', originally meaning armed for the pit. The football club is pure decoy.

clue.text: Cheese production initially stops its run (7)

blocks.note: just its first letter, which 'stops' — plugs — the gap
'it' = SA (sex appeal, the 'It' in It girl); the plural gives a pair of them
a run at something = a go at it

explanation.walkthrough: Sapsago is a hard green Swiss cheese. 'It' = SA is vintage crosswordese for sex appeal; Enigmatist pluralises it to get two, then the P stops the gap between them.

clue.text: Friend is one shot (5)

blocks.note: first person: is = am
the Roman numeral
have a shot = have a go

explanation.walkthrough: Read it as a tiny sentence: is = AM, one = I, shot = GO — and a Spanish friend appears.

clue.text: Dodge section that is recording (8)

blocks.note: s. — as in a legal citation
id est — 'that is' before it was abbreviated to i.e.
an extended-play record

explanation.walkthrough: The trick is 'that is' expanded to its full Latin, id est, rather than the usual two-letter i.e.

clue.text: Forest dweller there – fearfully symmetrical, according to recital (5)

blocks.note: Blake's 'Tyger Tyger, burning bright… thy fearful symmetry' points at the tiger, whose homophone doubles as the word for the great northern forest it prowls

explanation.walkthrough: The taiga is the great northern forest, and its most famous dweller arrives via Blake's poem — 'fearful symmetry' is the Tyger's own phrase, delivered 'according to recital'.

clue.text: Planet’s reporter takes chorus on leave, on the way to the Proms? (10,4)

blocks.note: italicised because it is a title: the Daily Planet, Superman's paper
Clark Kent, the Planet's reporter — split round the chorus
to chorus = to sing together; it sits inside KENT
the first 'on' spells itself
to leave = to go
the second 'on' = re, about

explanation.walkthrough: Kensington Gore is the road at the Royal Albert Hall, where the Proms play — and the name later became stage slang for fake blood. The italics flag Planet as a newspaper: Clark Kent's Daily Planet.
